samples.summary: New value-mismatch refusal is only tested at the cell layer; the sheet/column/row layer mismatch branches are untested
samples.evidence: The delta added `sheetValue !== value` (sheet.ts:4259), `colValue !== value` (4266) and `rowValue !== value` (4274) refusals that fire even when the selection OWNS the layer. Every new test exercises only the cell-level mismatch: 'should not strip a format another cell in the selection carries' (line 177) and 'should not strip decimals another cell in the selection set deeper' (line 207) put the disagreeing value in a cell style via setStyle, and 'should not strip a format a sheet-wide step would reach' (line 195) — despite its name — also disagrees at the cell (C3 nf:'percent'), while the sheetStyle values match. No test constructs an owned column/row/sheet layer holding a *different* dp/nf, so those three new branches could be deleted and the suite would stay green. I grepped the whole test tree for selectRow/selectAllCells/dp: (only formatting.test.ts, pivot-parse.test.ts, xlsx-styles.test.ts match, none call changeDecimals/unsetRangeStyleValues).

samples.summary: The new pre-scan-before-write atomicity guarantee has no test that would fail if writes went back to being interleaved with the scan
samples.evidence: The delta's stated purpose for hoisting the cell scan out of removeCellStyleKeysInRange is the comment at sheet.ts:4288 ('a single disagreeing cell still leaves the whole selection untouched'). In both refusal tests (decimals.test.ts:177 and :207) the cells that WOULD have been edited before the refusal hold their dp/nf in a range patch (A1 was empty when changeDecimals(1) ran), so nothing cell-level would have been written even under the old interleaved order; and the subsequent explicit setRangeStyle({dp:0}) rewrites the same cells anyway, masking any partial write. No test sets up an owned cell with extra keys (e.g. {b:true, dp:n, nf:'number'}) plus a later disagreeing cell and asserts the first cell is byte-identical afterwards, so the atomicity fix is asserted only by a comment.

finding.summary: Row-selection and whole-sheet ('all') branches of the new `unsetRangeStyleKeys` are never exercised by any test
finding.evidence: The new suite only covers cell (`selectStart`), multi-cell (`selectStart`+`selectEnd`) and column (`selectColumn(1)`) selections. Nothing calls `selectRow(...)` or `selectAll()/selectAllCells()`, so `sheet.ts:4256-4265` (row-style conflict check), `4300-4311` (row-style rewrite) and `4281-4287` (`ownsSheet && this.sheetStyle` rewrite) plus the `!ownsSheet && this.sheetStyle?.[key]` bail at `4243` are entirely uncovered — roughly half the branch surface of the new method. A regression in the row or sheet layer (e.g. writing the wrong key set, or clearing a row style the selection does not own) would keep the suite green.

verdict.reason: Partially refuted, not fully. The method is actually named `unsetRangeStyleValues` (sheet.ts:4238), and the reviewer's evidence that "nothing calls selectAll()/selectAllCells()" is false: decimals.test.ts:200 calls `sheet.selectAllCells()`, which sets `selectionType = 'all'` (sheet.ts:2979-2980), so the `ownsSheet` path at 4251-4261 is executed by that test. However the row half of the claim holds up: `unsetRangeStyleValues` has exactly one caller (`changeDecimals`, sheet.ts:4210); `changeDecimals` appears only in decimals.test.ts and src/view/spreadsheet.ts; the view wrappers are only used by packages/frontend/src/components/formatting-toolbar.tsx:249,253 which has no test; and `selectRow(` appears in tests only in formatting.test.ts:192,525,556,619, which never invokes decimals. So the row conflict check (4270-4277) and row rewrite (4340-4351) are never executed. Additionally the one 'all' test refuses the unset at the cell-level conflict (4306-4311, C3 has nf:'percent') and so never reaches the sheet rewrite at 4321-4327; inverting the `!ownsSheet ||` guard at 4259 would still leave that test green. Since a genuine uncovered branch remains and I found no counterexample for it, refuting would wrongly drop a real gap; but the finding's cited evidence is materially inaccurate, so I cannot confirm it as written either.
